description: §14.8.9 — declassification is COLUMN-keyed, not existence-keyed. `passwordHash` is the protected column; the body reveals `email`. That reveal declassifies nothing about `passwordHash`, so the raw-egress gate still fires E-PROTECT-004. The adversarial twin of `reveal-suppresses-e004`, which reveals the RIGHT column and is correctly silent.
rationale: §14.8.9: `reveal("col")` stamps THE NAMED COLUMN's provenance descriptor as declassified-at-this-value — it is a per-column admit, not a per-body switch. Until S405 the gate's suppression tested only for the PRESENCE of a `.reveal(` anywhere in the body, so revealing any column disarmed the gate for every protected column in that body: `reveal("email")` silently declassified `passwordHash`. This case pins the narrowed rule — the gate is discharged only when every protected OUTPUT column of the offending query is named by a reveal. It goes red against the pre-S405 emitter, which is what makes it a proof rather than a description. ⚑ S441 (`g-protected-column-escapes-redaction-as-scalar`): `I-PROTECT-STRIP-001` no longer co-fires here, because nothing is stripped — the info now fires only for a query whose row the egress sink ACTUALLY stripped (the §14.8.9 provenance flow, `compiler/src/codegen/protect-flow.ts`). Before S441 it fired for every protected SELECT, and this case pinned that false claim. `E-PROTECT-006` co-fires on the same column-keyed basis: `reveal("email")` does not declassify `passwordHash`, so `JSON.stringify` of the row serializes it naked into the response.
